Abbotsford Neighbourhood Guides: streets and boundaries

items.t: Abbotsford's neighbourhoods are mapped three different ways, and this hub page is where the three lists meet: the City's demographic profile areas, the Official Community Plan (OCP) neighbourhood plans, and the real estate board's sub-area names.
The City's 2020 Demographic Profiles number its communities, including Bradner – Mt. Lehman (area 1), Aberdeen (area 6) and West Abbotsford (area 7).
The OCP carries four named neighbourhood plans — City Centre, Historic Downtown, UDistrict and McKee — which do not cover the rural west side of the city at all.
Board sub-area names such as Aberdeen are used in Fraser Valley board data and do not always match a City profile area or an OCP plan area of the same name.

blocks.text: Abbotsford Neighbourhood Guides: the housing stock

items.t: The hub's neighbourhoods split into two stocks: urban neighbourhoods inside the urban development boundary, and rural farm communities such as Aberdeen and Bradner where the minimum subdivision lot area is 8.0 hectares (A1 zone) or 16.0 hectares (A2 zone).

McKee, the OCP's New Neighbourhoods area above Auguston and Highlands, is the city's planned growth neighbourhood: its plan area held about 4,600 people in 1,193 dwelling units when the plan was written.

blocks.text: Abbotsford Neighbourhood Guides: rules that affect buyers

items.t: Which rulebook applies depends on which map the lot falls: an OCP neighbourhood plan (City Centre, Historic Downtown, UDistrict, McKee) adds plan-level policy on top of Zoning Bylaw No. 2400-2014, while rural areas outside those plans run on the zoning bylaw and, on farm land, Agricultural Land Reserve rules.
A neighbourhood name alone never settles a lot's zone or floodplain status; the City's WebMap shows both for the specific parcel.

blocks.text: Abbotsford Neighbourhood Guides: local details a buyer would not know

items.t: The McKee Neighbourhood Plan area's existing neighbourhoods are Auguston and Highlands; "McKee" is the plan name for the hillside above them, not a separate older community.
Mill Lake Park, in the City Centre, is described in the City's Mill Lake Park Master Plan (2025) as the heart of the city's parks system and its premier urban park.
The City's 2022–2026 Strategic Plan records a completed Montrose Transit Exchange and an introduced McKee Neighbourhood Plan among its delivered items. Strategic Plan.pdf
Highstreet Transit Exchange, at Mt. Lehman Road, serves the west side neighbourhoods on BC Transit route 21; Bourquin Exchange serves the City Centre side.
Abbotsford Regional Hospital and Cancer Centre, 32900 Marshall Road, sits in the UDistrict side of the city and anchors that neighbourhood plan area.

blocks.text: Abbotsford Neighbourhood Guides: costs and taxes

items.t: The Speculation and Vacancy Tax applies in every Abbotsford neighbourhood: the Province's taxable-areas list names the City of Abbotsford as a whole, with no neighbourhood exceptions.
One transit system serves all Abbotsford neighbourhoods: BC Transit's Central Fraser Valley system, with exchanges at Bourquin, Clearbrook Centre, Highstreet and Montrose.
Route 21 Fraser Hwy is the cross-city link along Fraser Highway, connecting the west side neighbourhoods to Bourquin Exchange in the City Centre.
No Abbotsford neighbourhood has rapid transit; the nearest West Coast Express station is Mission City Station, across the Fraser River in Mission.

blocks.text: Abbotsford Neighbourhood Guides: risks and due diligence

items.t: The risk layers differ by neighbourhood type: floodplain (Zoning Bylaw Schedule E) on the lowland and Matsqui Prairie side, airport height surfaces (City drawing M-500) in the southwest, and Agricultural Land Reserve status across the rural west.
A hub page cannot settle any of those layers for a specific home; each is a parcel check in the City's WebMap or, for ALR land, on Agricultural Land Commission mapping.

faq.a: Because three different systems name it. The City profiles its communities as numbered demographic areas, the Official Community Plan names four plan areas (City Centre, Historic Downtown, UDistrict and McKee), and the real estate board uses its own sub-area names in its data. A listing's sub-area name, a City profile area and an OCP plan area can cover different ground, so check which system a claim comes from.
faq.q: Why does the same Abbotsford area have different names?

faq.a: Four do: City Centre, Historic Downtown, UDistrict and McKee are the neighbourhood plans named in the Official Community Plan. Everywhere else in the city — including the rural west side communities such as Aberdeen and Bradner — is governed by the city-wide OCP and Zoning Bylaw No. 2400-2014 without a neighbourhood plan layer.
faq.q: Which Abbotsford neighbourhoods have their own plan?

faq.a: In the School District No. 34 (SD34) School Locator, by exact address. Catchments are set under SD34 Policy 18 and follow street addresses, not neighbourhood or sub-area names, so two homes in the same named neighbourhood can feed different schools.
faq.q: Where do I check which school a neighbourhood feeds?

faq.a: The west side — Aberdeen, Bradner and Mt. Lehman — is rural farm country under the A1 and A2 agricultural zones, with subdivision minimums of 8.0 and 16.0 hectares. The urban neighbourhoods sit inside the urban development boundary around Clearbrook, the City Centre, Mill Lake and the McKee hillside, under urban residential zones such as RS3 and RS7. The City's own profile areas keep the two sets separate.
